_about: W18 S2 (W17-05): the questions a visitor can leave on Snowdrop's front desk in Classroom 2-B (src/world/places/deskQuestion.js), each tied to what she is reading or what the visitor has read. `about` = event-log ids that make it one of the offered cards (read:<note> = the visitor opened that note; place:<id> = they went there); `reading: true` = her paper on the desk now; `always` = offered to anyone. `short` is her Meet answer; `answer` is what she pencils under the slip when she reads it at the desk. Her own words about real papers: keep them true to the notes they cite.

questions.text: Three hundred tokens into an answer, is the picture still in the room?
questions.short: I don't know yet. That is the honest answer, and it is the whole project.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "I don't know yet. The image is read once, at the start; the words keep growing after that. My hunch is that the picture's pull fades as the answer gets long. A hunch is not a measurement."

Smaller, below it: "So I split it into things I can measure apart: how much attention the image still gets, and what happens to the answer when I take the image away. They may not fade together. Which one would convince you?"

questions.text: If the model's attention lands on the image, does that prove it used the image?
questions.short: No. Attention pools in some places just because it has to go somewhere.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "No. The first few tokens soak up attention whether they matter or not, like water stopping behind a rock. A big share on the image can be a sink, not a look."
Below it: "To show it used the picture, change the picture and see if the answer moves. That is why the blackboard runs take the second look away and give it back."

questions.text: Why do long-context models miss what sits in the middle?
questions.short: They do best at the two ends of the corridor and worst halfway down. Why is still open.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "Liu and the others moved the one useful passage around a long input. Accuracy was best with it at the start or the end, worst in the middle: a U."
Below it: "Why, nobody has fully pinned down. For me it is a baseline: before I say the image fades late in an answer, I have to rule out plain position."

questions.text: Can a model that describes a whole street really fail to count two crossing lines?
questions.short: Yes. Describing a scene and seeing exact geometry are different skills.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "BlindTest asks what a child answers at a glance: do two lines cross, do two circles touch. Strong models got many of them wrong, and sounded sure."
Below it: "My guess is the image is squeezed small before the words ever see it, and fine geometry gets lost there. It is a guess. That's why it's in pencil."

questions.text: If the depth camera is missing, why not just feed the model zeros?
questions.short: Because zero is a value. The network still hears it.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "A layer with a bias turns zero into something that is not zero. A zero-filled depth image is not absence; it is a grey panel the model never trained on."
Below it: "Measure with that and you mix two costs: losing the depth, and being shown something strange. I wanted a test that only takes the first."

questions.text: Can a model lean in and look at the picture a second time?
questions.short: Most can't: the picture is read once. V* gave a model that move on purpose.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "Usually the image is encoded once, small, and everything after happens in words. Wu and Xie gave the model a search step: decide where to look, then look closer."
Below it: "That turns 'does it look again' from a metaphor into a switch you can flip. Then you can test it. I like questions that become switches."

questions.text: When a model writes out its reasoning, is that really how it got the answer?
questions.short: Sometimes. You find out by changing the reasoning and watching the answer.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "Lanham and the others cut the reasoning short, slipped mistakes into it, paraphrased it. When the answer never changes, the reasoning was decoration."
Below it: "It varied a lot from task to task. Correct and faithful are different things, so I keep them in two columns."

questions.text: Why do the seedlings curl under the grow-lamps?
questions.short: When the low tide dims the city, the grow-lamps dim with it, and the leaves keep count.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "When the low tide dims the city, the grow-lamps dim too. A seedling doesn't care why. It only gets less light, and curls."
Below it: "I'm mapping which trays curl most. If the dips were random, the curl would be too. So far it isn't."

questions.text: Why do you read papers aloud to an empty classroom?
questions.short: So I can hear where an argument skips a step.
answer: Under your slip, in pencil: "Reading aloud is slower. When a sentence skips a step, my voice trips on it before my eyes do."
Below it, smaller: "And the room isn't empty now, is it."
